description: A team of 12-year-old students bound to take over the universe.
summary: Mission: Bring Everyone Home is a 3D browser game about planning a space mission when things go wrong. Three astronauts and their three alien pups are on a damaged ship. Before launch the player packs cargo with a limited mass and budget. Then they seal a hull breach, share out too little power between ship systems, and choose a route home that trades fuel against days of supplies. At the end, a mission report shows how each choice changed the outcome. Everyone always gets home. The choices decide how close it was and whether the science samples survive.
details:
What it does

The player leads a crew of three astronauts on the ship Juniper:

  • Nova, flight engineer. She does repairs: drives bolts, reseats cables and fits parts.
  • Lyra, systems specialist. She scans consoles and equipment to find out what is really wrong.
  • Orion, navigator. He is small enough for crawlspaces and hatches, and he plots the routes home.

Three alien pups come too: Pixel, Comet and Sprout. They wear suits and helmets, they sniff out useful parts, and you can give them a pat.

The game is in five parts:

  1. Launch day (flashback, six weeks earlier). Pre-flight checks done as a team: tighten a fuel coupling, run a scan, free Sprout's toy from a crawlspace. Then pack the ship at the cargo loader. There are six items and the hold allows 100 mass and 80 credits, so you cannot take everything:
    • Repair kit (20 mass, 15 credits): a ready patch panel for Level 1 and a spare antenna part for Level 3.
    • Battery pack (25 mass, 20 credits): 2 extra power units in Level 2.
    • Science kit (30 mass, 30 credits): a sample freezer. This is the reason for the trip.
    • Spare fuel (35 mass, 25 credits): +30 fuel, which makes the fast direct route possible.
    • Supply crate (20 mass, 10 credits): +35 days of supplies, needed for the long route.
    • Comms booster (10 mass, 15 credits): makes the radio dish easier to aim. You can also fly with an empty hold. The game then makes you salvage parts from the ship.
  2. Level 1: Seal the ship. An impact breaches the airlock. Lyra scans the breach to learn what is needed: a patch panel, a fastening tool and sealant. Some tasks need two crew members at once, such as one holding the panel while another lines it up. Floating junk (a sock, a cracked tablet, a bent spoon, a squeaky toy) looks useful but is not, and the game says why. Without the repair kit, Orion crawls behind a service hatch to salvage a spare hull plate. The level ends with a Seal Check: hold a button to pump air into the airlock and let go inside the target band. Too much air opens the safety valve and you try again.
    • Life support: never below 2, because the crew and pets need air. At 3, efficient scrubbers make supplies last 6 days longer.
    • Lighting (0 to 2): emergency strips, dim lights or full lights.
    • Communications (0 to 2): needs at least 1 to call home. More power gives a stronger signal and an easier dish to aim.
    • Navigation (0 to 2): needs at least 1. At 1, two simple routes can be planned. At 2, the gravity-assist route opens too.
    • Mission equipment (0 to 2, only with the science kit): powers the sample freezer. At 0 the samples spoil. The lights and machines in the room change as you move the power around, and you can change your mind before you confirm. These choices carry on into Level 3: a dark bridge if lighting got nothing, a harder dish if comms is weak.
    • Direct burn: 80 fuel, 30 days. Only possible with the spare fuel.
    • Balanced transfer: 55 fuel, 60 days.
    • Gravity assist past the Moon: 35 fuel, 95 days. Needs navigation at full power and enough supplies. A route is marked "Not possible" with the reason, for example "Takes 95 days, supplies last 65." The level ends with the Departure Burn: hold to fire the engine and let go inside the window. Too long and the flight computer resets the burn.
  3. Everyone home. Earth approach, docking at a station, helmets off and a celebration. Then a mission report shows crew safety, the route taken, fuel and days left over (rated Generous, Comfortable or Thin), the power plan, the loadout carried, whether the original science goal was kept or lost, how many pieces of junk were picked up, and a list called "What your choices changed". The player can then "Fly again with another plan".

Controls: WASD to move, E to use or talk, Tab or 1 to 3 to switch astronaut, Esc to pause. Arrow keys aim the dish. On a touch screen there is an on-screen stick, an action button and portraits to tap. Walk up to a crewmate to talk, ask them to wait or follow, take over, or high five.

How it works

It is a single-page web app built with Vite and Three.js. The ship, the crew, the pups and the rooms are built in code from Three.js shapes and materials, not loaded as 3D model files. Sound effects and background sound are made live in the browser with the Web Audio API, not played from audio files. 2D art is used for the character portraits (neutral, happy and concerned faces), cargo item cards, story stills (launch day, the breach, the homecoming), a nebula backdrop, key art and a mission patch emblem.

The mission numbers are kept in one small set of rules: item mass and cost, power units per cell, what each power level unlocks, starting fuel and supplies, and each route's fuel and days. The mission report reads the player's saved choices and explains them in plain sentences.

Progress is saved in the browser with checkpoints. Players can continue later, restart a level (finished repairs stay done) or quit to the menu. The site is hosted on Cloudflare Workers.

Benefits

  • It shows that mission planning is about trade-offs. Mass, money, power, fuel and time are all limited, and a choice early on changes what is possible later.
  • It shows teamwork. Each astronaut has one job, and some tasks need two people at once.
  • It explains failure kindly. When something does not work, the game says why and lets you try again. Nobody is lost: the question is how well the mission went, not whether the crew survived.
  • It says clearly that its numbers are not real: "Fuel, power and supply numbers are simplified for learning. They are not real flight planning."

Intended impact

[To confirm with the team. Suggested, based on the game: help younger players understand why real missions plan cargo, power and routes so carefully, and get them curious about how real spacecraft are designed. Do not claim it has been tested with players unless it has.]

Tools, languages and software

  • JavaScript, HTML and CSS
  • Three.js (3D graphics)
  • Vite (build tool)
  • Web Audio API (sound made in the browser)
  • Fonts: Audiowide, Space Grotesk and Space Mono
  • Cloudflare Workers (hosting)
  • [Other tools used to make the art, for example drawing or image software: to confirm]
  • [Source repository link: to add]

Creativity

  • The pups are not only cute. They are part of the story: they need protection when the ship is open to space, they sniff out the useful parts, and the game checks they stayed safe.
  • Each astronaut has a body that matters: Orion is small, so only he fits into crawlspaces.
  • Silly junk (a sock, a spoon, a squeaky toy) floats around to teach "real parts only". The game even counts how much junk you picked up.
  • Choices carry across levels. The cargo packed on launch day decides which routes exist at the end, and the power plan decides how dark the bridge is and how hard the dish is to aim.
  • The same mission can end in different ways, so the game invites a second try with a different plan.

Factors considered

  • Accessibility. A settings menu has Sound on/off, Reduced motion, Captions and Graphics quality (High or Low). Reduced motion turns on by default if the device asks for it, and it also slows down the timing mini-games. Captions are on by default. Graphics start on Low on touch devices. Menus are labelled for screen readers.
  • Keyboard and touch. Both are supported, with controls listed on the main menu and in the pause menu.
  • Age and tone. Friendly characters, short sentences, gentle humour, no scary failures.
  • Honesty about the science. The numbers are simplified, and the game says so in the mission report.
  • Saving. Checkpoints mean a player can stop and come back.
  • Browsers. If WebGL is missing, the page explains what is needed instead of failing silently.
